DragDiffusion thus combines several prior ideas, including inversion, an intermediate step as the place of layout, a light fine-tuning as identity anchor, and mutual self-attention, and shows that diffusion features are discriminative enough to serve as their own tracker, as DIFT [@tang2023dift] also exploits. Dragging has since moved into video models and into commercial editing tools, which is the clearest case in this chapter of a research interface becoming a product one.

## Textual Inversion: a new word for a new concept {#sec-ti}

Personalisation asks the model to render one particular object or style that no prompt describes precisely. Textual Inversion [@gal2023ti] keeps the generator frozen and learns, from 3--5 images, the embedding of a pseudo-word $S_*$ that can then be used in any sentence ("an oil painting of $S_*$", "a $S_*$ backpack"; @fig-ti-teaser).

![**Textual Inversion.** A pseudo-word $S_*$ found from a few images of a sculpture or a toy places the concept in new scenes, styles and products. Reproduced from [@gal2023ti, Fig. 1].](figures/lec11/PhuTran1005-ti-teaser.png){#fig-ti-teaser width=80%}

A latent diffusion model is trained with
$$
L_{LDM} = \mathbb{E}_{z \sim \mathcal{E}(x),\, y,\, \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1),\, t}\Big[\big\lVert \epsilon - \epsilon_\theta\big(z_t, t, c_\theta(y)\big) \big\rVert_2^2\Big],
$$ {#eq-ti-ldm}
where the text encoder $c_\theta$ maps each token of the prompt $y$ to an embedding vector and processes the sequence with a transformer. Textual Inversion gives the placeholder $S_*$ a free embedding $v$ and solves
$$
v_* = \arg\min_v\ \mathbb{E}_{z \sim \mathcal{E}(x),\, y,\, \epsilon,\, t}\Big[\big\lVert \epsilon - \epsilon_\theta\big(z_t, t, c_\theta(y, v)\big) \big\rVert_2^2\Big],
$$ {#eq-ti}
over the concept images $x$ and neutral templates $y$ such as "a photo of $S_*$", with everything but $v$ frozen. The gradient $\nabla_v L = (\partial c_\theta/\partial v)^\top (\partial \epsilon_\theta/\partial c)^\top\, 2(\epsilon_\theta - \epsilon)$ reaches $v$ only through the cross-attention layers and the frozen text transformer. Because the objective is reconstruction, the vector captures visual detail; because $v$ is an input of the text transformer, every new sentence contextualises it like any other word, which is why one vector composes with arbitrary prompts. The paper's model is a 1.4-billion-parameter LDM (1280-dimensional embeddings; 768 for Stable Diffusion); the vector is initialised from a coarse word ("sculpture") and optimised for 5,000 steps, about an hour per concept, and occupies a few kilobytes.

The variants trace a distortion--editability trade-off familiar from GAN inversion [@tov2021e4e] (@tbl-ti): more vectors barely improve reconstruction and hurt editability, pulling the vector towards a real word does the opposite, and human-written captions are worse on both axes --- hence the title, "an image is worth one word". About five images with varied backgrounds work best. Exact shapes are hard to capture (the learned token covers 75.8 % of style concepts but only 34.3 % of objects), relations between two concepts fail, and on Stable Diffusion the embeddings tend to dominate the prompt, which the authors attribute to its frozen CLIP text encoder.

| Variant | Reconstruction | Editability |
|---|---|---|
| one vector (default) | 0.79 | 0.27 |
| two or three vectors | 0.80 | 0.24 |
| regularised towards the coarse word | 0.73 | 0.28 |
| human-written long captions | 0.62 | 0.23 |

: CLIP-based reconstruction and editability of Textual Inversion variants (reproduced values from Gal et al. [@gal2023ti]). {#tbl-ti}

Set beside @sec-nulltext, the pair makes the method's shape clear. Both
optimise a text embedding of a frozen model against a reconstruction loss, and
both leave the weights alone; they differ in what the embedding has to be good
for. Null-text inversion fits one image and needs the result only at the
timestep it was fitted at, so it can afford a different vector per step.
Textual Inversion fits a concept and needs the result to survive being placed
in sentences it has never seen, so it gets one vector and a prior-shaped
initialisation. The lecture added a caveat that applies to both: on DiT
architectures and flow models the inversion step is done differently, so the
mechanism here should be read for the idea rather than the recipe.

## DreamBooth: binding a rare token by fine-tuning {#sec-dreambooth}

DreamBooth [@ruiz2023dreambooth] takes the opposite route and fine-tunes all weights on 3--5 images of a subject, so that a rare token $[V]$ comes to mean that subject, which can then be shown in new contexts, poses and lighting with a fidelity a word embedding cannot reach (@fig-dreambooth-teaser).

![**DreamBooth.** From four photos of a corgi puppy, the fine-tuned model shows the same dog in the Acropolis, swimming, sleeping, in a bucket and getting a haircut. Reproduced from [@ruiz2023dreambooth, Fig. 1].](figures/lec11/PhuTran1005-dreambooth-teaser.png){#fig-dreambooth-teaser width=80%}

### The objective and the identifier

DreamBooth writes the model in **$x$-prediction** form with amplitudes $\alpha_t, \sigma_t$ and text condition $c$:
$$
\mathbb{E}_{x, c, \epsilon, t}\Big[w_t\, \big\lVert \hat x_\theta(\alpha_t x + \sigma_t \epsilon,\ c) - x \big\rVert_2^2\Big].
$$ {#eq-db-loss}
This is the noise-prediction loss up to a weight: if the network predicts $\hat\epsilon$, then $\hat x = (z_t - \sigma_t \hat\epsilon)/\alpha_t$ and
$$
\hat x - x = \frac{\alpha_t x + \sigma_t \epsilon - \sigma_t \hat\epsilon}{\alpha_t} - x = -\frac{\sigma_t}{\alpha_t}\,(\hat\epsilon - \epsilon),
\qquad
w_t \lVert \hat x - x \rVert_2^2 = \frac{w_t}{\mathrm{SNR}_t}\, \lVert \hat\epsilon - \epsilon \rVert_2^2, \quad \mathrm{SNR}_t = \frac{\alpha_t^2}{\sigma_t^2},
$$ {#eq-db-equiv}
so the plain $\epsilon$-loss of Stable Diffusion corresponds to $w_t = \mathrm{SNR}_t$. All images are labelled "a [V] [class noun]"; the class noun ties the subject to the class prior, which supplies shape and plausible poses (subject fidelity drops from a DINO score of 0.744 to 0.303 without it). The identifier should carry a weak prior: English words have meanings to unlearn and random strings split into letters, so DreamBooth samples rare tokens of the vocabulary. Unlike Textual Inversion, the token's embedding is not optimised; the model is fine-tuned to give it a meaning. The lecture presented the procedure as Textual Inversion followed by fine-tuning with the text held fixed, which is a natural reading of the two papers in sequence but not what DreamBooth does. There is no inversion stage and no learned embedding: $[V]$ is picked from the vocabulary before training starts and never moves. The distinction matters for the comparison in @tbl-ti-db, because it is what makes DreamBooth's cost a whole checkpoint rather than a vector.

### Language drift and the prior-preservation loss

Naive fine-tuning causes language drift (the model forgets the class, and "a dog" produces the subject) and reduced diversity. DreamBooth therefore lets the frozen model generate about 1,000 samples $x_{\mathrm{pr}}$ of "a [class noun]" (condition $c_{\mathrm{pr}}$) and keeps reconstructing them:
$$
\mathbb{E}_{x, c, \epsilon, \epsilon', t}\Big[w_t \big\lVert \hat x_\theta(\alpha_t x + \sigma_t \epsilon, c) - x \big\rVert_2^2
+ \lambda\, w_{t'} \big\lVert \hat x_\theta(\alpha_{t'} x_{\mathrm{pr}} + \sigma_{t'} \epsilon', c_{\mathrm{pr}}) - x_{\mathrm{pr}} \big\rVert_2^2\Big].
$$ {#eq-db-ppl}
The second term is rehearsal: with ELBO weighting integrated over $t$, it upper-bounds a Monte-Carlo estimate of $\mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_{\mathrm{pre}}}[-\log p_\theta(x \mid c_{\mathrm{pr}})] = H(p_{\mathrm{pre}}) + D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{\mathrm{pre}} \Vert p_\theta)$, with $p_{\mathrm{pre}}$ the frozen model's class distribution, so it keeps the class distribution close to the original while the first term moves "a [V] dog" to the subject (with the $\epsilon$-loss weighting used in practice this is a heuristic, not a bound).

On a benchmark of 30 subjects and 25 prompts, with subject fidelity measured by DINO [@caron2021dino] and CLIP image similarity and prompt fidelity by CLIP text similarity, DreamBooth clearly beats Textual Inversion (@tbl-db), and users preferred it for subject fidelity in 68 % against 22 % of the answers. Without prior preservation, generated "a dog" images become similar to the subject (PRES 0.664 against 0.493) and diversity drops, at a slightly higher subject fidelity. The limitations are rare contexts, appearance changing with the context, overfitting, and a full model copy per subject.

| Method | DINO $\uparrow$ | CLIP-I $\uparrow$ | CLIP-T $\uparrow$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| real images (upper bound) | 0.774 | 0.885 | --- |
| DreamBooth (Imagen) | **0.696** | **0.812** | **0.306** |
| DreamBooth (Stable Diffusion) | 0.668 | 0.803 | 0.305 |
| Textual Inversion (Stable Diffusion) | 0.569 | 0.780 | 0.255 |

: Subject and prompt fidelity, Table 1 of Ruiz et al. [@ruiz2023dreambooth]. {#tbl-db}

The two methods are ends of a spectrum (@tbl-ti-db). In between lie partial fine-tuning methods such as LoRA [@hu2022lora] (DragDiffusion's identity-preserving step is a single-image LoRA-DreamBooth) and Custom Diffusion [@kumari2023custom], which tunes only the cross-attention keys and values. Moving towards full fine-tuning increases fidelity, cost and the risk of drift.

| | Textual Inversion | DreamBooth |
|--|---|----|
| what is optimised | one word embedding | all U-Net weights (860 M for SD) |
| identifier | new token, learned embedding | existing rare token plus class noun |
| regulariser | none (model frozen) | class prior preservation |
| storage per concept | a few KB | a full checkpoint |
| typical failure | imprecise shape | language drift, overfitting |

: Two ends of the personalisation spectrum. {#tbl-ti-db}

## Synthesis: what the lecture teaches as a whole {#sec-edit-synthesis}

**1. Where to intervene.** Training-free methods (Prompt-to-Prompt, Plug-and-Play, MasaCtrl) are cheap but limited to what the frozen model does in one pass; per-image optimisation (Null-text inversion, DragDiffusion) buys fidelity to a real image for about a minute; trained modules (GLIGEN, ControlNet, Asyrp's $f_t$) add a control once and for all; fine-tuning (InstructPix2Pix, DreamBooth) changes what the model knows.

@tbl-edit-methods puts the eleven in one place first, by what the user supplies
and what the method actually changes.

| Method | What the user supplies | What is changed or learned |
|---|---|---|
| Asyrp | a semantic direction, e.g. "smiling" | bottleneck shift $\Delta h_t$, applied asymmetrically |
| Null-text inversion | a real image and its caption | per-step null embeddings $\varnothing_t$ |
| Prompt-to-Prompt | a source and an edited prompt | cross-attention maps during sampling |
| InstructPix2Pix | an image and an instruction | the model, retrained on generated pairs |
| Plug-and-Play | an image and a target prompt | injected features and self-attention maps |
| GLIGEN | a caption, phrases and boxes | added gated self-attention layers |
| ControlNet | a prompt and a spatial map | a trainable encoder copy behind zero convolutions |
| MasaCtrl | an image and a changed action | target queries read source keys and values |
| DragDiffusion | an image, handle and target points | a LoRA, then one intermediate latent |
| Textual Inversion | a few images of a concept | one token embedding $v$ |
| DreamBooth | a few images of a subject | all weights, with prior preservation |

: The eleven methods by interface and by what each one moves. {#tbl-edit-methods}

Read down the last column and the chapter's argument is visible in one view:
the thing being changed moves steadily outwards, from a hidden feature to an
embedding, to attention, to an added module, to the weights themselves, and
the cost rises with it.

**2. Early steps decide layout, late steps appearance.** Almost every method encodes this in a schedule (@tbl-schedules); structure-preserving methods act early, appearance-preserving MasaCtrl acts late.

| Method | Intervention in time |
|--|----|
| Asyrp | edit on $[T, t_{\mathrm{edit}}]$, $t_{\mathrm{edit}} \approx 300$--$500$ of 1000 |
| Prompt-to-Prompt / Plug-and-Play | inject maps or features in the first 50--80 % of the steps |
| GLIGEN | grounding layers active in the first 20--30 % of the steps |
| MasaCtrl | mutual self-attention from step 4 of 50 |
| DragDiffusion | optimise the latent at step 35 of 50 |
| this chapter (@fig-xattn) | the "burger" map is fixed after about 6 of 50 steps |

: Where the methods place their interventions in time. {#tbl-schedules}

**3. Inversion is the gateway to real images, and guidance makes it hard** (@sec-edit-cfg, @tbl-edit-toy). Null-text inversion corrects the guided trajectory step by step; DragDiffusion turns guidance off and adds a LoRA; Plug-and-Play and MasaCtrl invert with the empty prompt, for which conditional and unconditional predictions coincide, and use guidance only in the target branch.

**4. Attention splits into where and what.** Prompt-to-Prompt borrows cross-attention maps, Plug-and-Play self-attention queries and keys, MasaCtrl and DragDiffusion keys and values (@tbl-duality, @fig-duality).

**5. New modules should start as the identity.** Methods that attach a branch to the pretrained generation path make its output zero at initialisation while keeping a gradient on its output-side parameter (@prp-gate, @prp-zeroconv; @tbl-identity), as do ADM's zero-initialised layers and DiT's adaLN-Zero [@peebles2023dit]. Asyrp's $f_t$, randomly initialised but acting only inside the editing interval, is an exception.

| Method | New component | Zero-initialised parameter |
|---|---|---|
| InstructPix2Pix | 4 extra input channels | their first-convolution weights |
| GLIGEN | gated self-attention | gate $\gamma$ in $\tanh(\gamma)$ |
| ControlNet | trainable encoder copy | zero convolutions |
| LoRA | low-rank update $BA$ | factor $B$ |

: The "start as identity" principle. {#tbl-identity}

**6. Fidelity and editability trade off everywhere.** Textual Inversion's distortion--editability curve, DreamBooth's prior preservation, InstructPix2Pix's $s_I$, Prompt-to-Prompt's injection fraction, MasaCtrl's start step and SDEdit's noise level are all knobs on one axis: how close the result stays to the source or the pretrained model, against how far the edit can go.

## How the worked examples were run {#sec-repro}

The chapter's central worked example is the two-dimensional reproduction of
null-text inversion (@sec-toy, @tbl-edit-toy, @fig-toy-nulltext). What makes it
possible is that for a Gaussian mixture the exact noise predictor is available
in closed form, so no network has to be trained and no approximation stands
between the claim and the measurement. That predictor is the whole of the
trick, and it is eight lines:

```{.python}
def eps_mix(x, a, logits, shift):
    """Exact E[eps | x_t = x] when x_0 follows a Gaussian mixture."""
    var = a * S**2 + (1 - a)                   # variance of the noisy mixture
    diff = x[None] - math.sqrt(a) * (MU + shift[None])
    logp = logits - diff.pow(2).sum(1) / (2 * var)
    r = torch.softmax(logp, 0)                 # responsibilities
    return math.sqrt(1 - a) * (r[:, None] * diff).sum(0) / var
```

The noisy marginal of a mixture of Gaussians is again a mixture, with means
$\sqrt{\alpha_t}\mu_k$ and variance $\alpha_t s^2 + 1 - \alpha_t$; the
responsibilities $r$ are the posterior over components given $x_t$, and the
score is their weighted average, which @eq-ddim-pd then turns into a noise
prediction. The conditional model is the same function with the components
outside the class given a logit of $-\infty$, and the "null embedding" of the
experiment is six parameters of the unconditional one --- four mixture logits
and a common shift of the means --- exact at their initial values, so that the
only thing optimisation can do is what null-text optimisation does.

The rest of the code for both experiments is in the book's repository under
[`code/ch12/`](https://github.com/bispl-website/ai618-textbook/tree/main/code/ch12):
the full sampler, inversion and per-step optimisation that produce
@tbl-edit-toy, and the script that evaluates the shift coefficients behind
@prp-asyrp-grid and @fig-asyrp-coeff.

### The Stable Diffusion experiments

The experiments of @fig-xattn and @fig-duality use Stable Diffusion v1.4 in float32 with the DDIM scheduler (scaled-linear betas 0.00085--0.012, `steps_offset=1`), 50 steps and $w = 7.5$. The three editing methods are implemented by one attention processor on the batch `[source-uncond, target-uncond, source-cond, target-cond]`: Prompt-to-Prompt copies the source's cross-attention probabilities (first 80 % of the steps) and self-attention probabilities at resolution $32 \times 32$ or lower (first 40 %); Plug-and-Play copies the source's self-attention queries and keys in decoder layers 4--11 (first 50 %) and, through a forward hook on `up_blocks[1].resnets[1].conv2`, its residual features (first 80 %), with the source prompt as negative prompt at weight $0.75(1 - i/49)$; MasaCtrl copies the source's keys and values in transformer blocks 10--15 from step 4. The seeds are 8888 (@fig-xattn) and 1234 (@fig-duality), applied to `torch.randn(1, 4, 64, 64)` through `torch.Generator().manual_seed`. On one shared B200 GPU each edit took about 10 s.

## Connections and further reading

* **Background and theory.** DDIM and its ODE view [@ddim; @sde], guidance [@ho2022cfg], latent diffusion [@rombach2022ldm], SDEdit [@meng2022sdedit] and *Geometry of Deep Learning* [@gdl]; DiffusionCLIP [@kim2022diffusionclip] precedes Asyrp.
* **Inversion.** Negative-prompt inversion [@miyake2023npi], Direct Inversion [@ju2024direct] and EDICT [@wallace2023edict] are faster or exact alternatives to Null-text inversion; Imagic [@kawar2023imagic] edits by fine-tuning.
* **Attention and correspondence.** StyleAligned [@hertz2024stylealigned], Text2Video-Zero [@khachatryan2023t2vzero] and TokenFlow [@geyer2024tokenflow] reuse the attention operators of MasaCtrl and Plug-and-Play; DIFT [@tang2023dift] explains why diffusion features match across images.
* **Control and personalisation.** T2I-Adapter [@mou2023t2iadapter], Custom Diffusion [@kumari2023custom], LoRA [@hu2022lora] and MagicBrush [@zhang2023magicbrush].
